title: The Resurrection and the Life: Why Jesus Waits and Weeps
speaker: Pastor Jonathan Landry Cruze
summary: This sermon examines John 11 and the raising of Lazarus to explore why Jesus delays and how His compassion and power work together. Pastor Cruze demonstrates that Jesus waits to glorify God and strengthen faith, and that His weeping at the tomb reveals His deep care for His people alongside His divine power. The passage assures believers that Jesus can be trusted in their suffering and calls them to faith in Him as the resurrection and the life.

outline.title: Why Does Jesus Wait?
subpoints: Jesus waits so that God will be glorified through a greater demonstration of power
Jesus waits so that the faith of His disciples and followers will be strengthened
Faith grows in the furnace of affliction and the anvil of anguish
Jesus calls Martha to faith in His person, not merely in future resurrection events

outline.title: Why Does Jesus Weep?
subpoints: Jesus weeps to demonstrate His complete compassion and care for suffering people
Jesus possesses both all power and all pity—omnipotence joined with mercy
His weeping propels His power to act on behalf of those He loves
Jesus is not a cold solution but the friend of sinners and man of sorrows

outline.title: The Call of Jesus in the Gospel
subpoints: Jesus's voice calling Lazarus from the grave is a picture of His calling sinners from spiritual death
Before Jesus calls us from the sleep of death, He calls us from the death of sin
His voice awakens us to new life and assures us of resurrection
The example of William Cowper shows how John 11 reveals Jesus's mercy to the broken and despairing

outline.title: The Hope of Resurrection in Christ
subpoints: Death has been transformed into a sleep for believers in Christ
Jesus will call believers by name on the last day and awaken them to eternal life
Jesus's resurrection differs from Lazarus's—He will never die again
Believers in Christ will experience a resurrection like Jesus's, not subject to death again

outline.title: Trust in God's Delayed Answers and Suffering
subpoints: Jesus only permits suffering after determining to perform deliverance from it
Unanswered prayers and delays may be preparing believers for greater redemption
If Jesus has solved the problem of death, He will solve all lesser sufferings
Believers should view troubles in light of eternity and God's ultimate plan

transcript:
## The Setting: A Personal Question About God

Where is God? That could be a theological question, a philosophical question, or an existential question. But I imagine for at least somebody in this church today, it's a very personal question. And when it's a personal question, it takes on a different flavor. It's not just where is God? It's where is God when I need him? Why didn't God show up when I needed him most?

Perhaps that's you this morning. You're going through some trials, some deep pain, suffering, some confusion, uncertain of the future. You've been praying and you feel like the Lord just hasn't showed up. Maybe you're here and you've been sort of flirting with the idea of Christianity and yet already you've been disappointed by the God that you thought was able to answer prayer. Now you're starting to wonder, what's it all about? What's this whole Christianity business about? Why should I be reading my Bible and why should I be praying before meals? Why should I be doing this and doing that, and not doing these things and not doing those things if the Lord isn't gonna show up when I need him?

Maybe you're asking that very critical question today. It's the question that Mary and Martha ask of Jesus. Where were you? Where were you when we needed you most?

That's a question we wanna ask along with them this morning. What I want to show you, friends, is that waiting on God is never, ever a waste. And not only is it not a waste, but what we learn from this text is that at times, Jesus causes us to wait in order to show us his power and his love in a way that we would never have seen otherwise. Sometimes Jesus calls us to wait and causes us to wait in order to demonstrate to us his power, but also his love in a way that we never would have seen otherwise.

## Why Does Jesus Wait?

That's the first question of our text. Mary and Martha are gonna both ask it in due course, but you might notice that the answer is already given before Jesus ever even gets to Bethany. This answer is anticipated in something that Jesus says to his disciples.

If you look back to the beginning of this chapter, news has come to him that a dear friend of his has fallen ill. Notice what Jesus says in verse four. Here is the beginning of the answer to the question why Jesus waits:

> "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God so that the Son of God may be glorified through it." (John 11:4)

This illness does not lead to death. Now this is not naive optimism, but this is divine omniscience. Jesus is speaking out of the infinite wealth of his knowledge as the eternal Son of God to reveal the true state of things that are hidden from human sight. When he says this illness does not lead to death, he's saying this will not ultimately lead to death. In fact, we know it will ultimately lead to a resurrection, and that resurrection will be the cause of God's being glorified. For the glory of God so that the Son of God may be glorified.

D.A. Carson says that it's the Father's express purpose that all should honor the Son even as they honor the Father, and the Father and the Son are mutually committed to one another's glory. So this is actually about the glory of God that the Son of God may be glorified through what is about to take place.

This is the first answer to why Jesus waits. Instead of immediately packing up their bags and heading to Bethany so that he could be with his dear friend and offer help, the answer is that God will be glorified in the waiting. God will be glorified in the waiting. That's the first answer, and let's be honest, it's the ultimate answer for everything. It's the ultimate answer for whatever you might be dealing with right now. It's the reason that God might be delaying in your life and delaying in coming to you. It's the reason for your suffering. It's the reason for your tears. It's the reason for the hardships that you're going through. God is to be glorified.

If we wanna be good Presbyterians and actually believe what we say we believe—that we are made to glorify God—then that means we don't want God to be just a little glorified, which is such a contradiction in terms it's meaningless. There is no such thing as glorifying God a little. Rather, we want God to be maximally glorified. And if that means it will come through suffering, we say, so be it. So be it.

Jesus here knows that the Father and the Son will receive more glory by raising a dead man from the grave than by raising a sick man off his bed. So, dear friend, this morning, if you feel perhaps lower than you have ever felt before, if you are in a pit that is deeper than you could have ever imagined, if the weight of suffering feels like it's crushing you, I wanna encourage you with this: If you are in Christ, then just imagine the soaring heights of the rescue and redemption that are sure and soon to come. Sometimes he waits, and the pain is so deep and the hurt is so heavy, so that the redemption will be all the more glorious.

### Faith Has a Growing Quality

Now, why else does Jesus wait? It's not just for his glory, but notice it's for the faith of his people. That's the second reason he gives. He says that both his disciples and he'll say it to Martha. Look at verse 15:

> "And for your sake, I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe." (John 11:15)

God glorifies himself in order to be believed on. God reveals himself in glorious ways in the world so that people would believe. And Jesus says, I'm glad that Lazarus has died for your sake so that you would believe.

Now that's an interesting thing to say to disciples who already believe in him. They believe in the Lord, they believe in his Messiah, they've given up everything to follow Christ. And yet Jesus says that this is that you would believe. It teaches us that faith has a growing quality, right? That faith is a progressive thing. There are new depths of faith to be plumbed, new heights of faith to be scaled. And the raising of Lazarus will have a profound effect on these disciples and would give their faith a content that it would not have otherwise.

And perhaps right now as I say that you are able to look back in your life on some of the difficult things the Lord has brought you through and some of the answers to prayer that he's provided. You can say, if it wasn't for those things, my faith would not be as strong as it is today. You look back and what are we called to do in the hymn? To raise our Ebenezer's, right? To say these are the moments in which God showed up and he answered in a marvelous way. As you do that, you recognize if I didn't have that difficulty, I wouldn't have the trust that I have today. Would you trust the Lord as deeply as you do now if it wasn't for the many answers to prayer you've received over the years? Or the many ways in which he providentially directed your steps to give you the very thing you needed?

God is in the business of growing our faith. He wants our faith to grow, grow and grow. But unfortunately for us, faith often grows best in the midst of suffering, in the midst of trial, seasons where we finally realize the only place that we can turn to for help is God himself.

Faith is sort of like a loaf of bread. It grows in the oven, in the heat. But friends, if that's for you today, don't be scared. It means God's forming something marvelous in you. Faith, when formed by God's spirit, even if it's in the furnace of affliction or upon the anvil of anguish, it will never fail you. It will never let you down. But that faith, it needs to be in Jesus Christ.

### Faith Must Be in Jesus Christ

That's additional light that Jesus brings to this question when Martha asks us. So if we look now to verse 21, she's asking the same question:

> "Lord, if you'd been here, my brother would not have died." (John 11:21)

She's saying, you know, where were you? Why did you wait so long? And Jesus says to her in verse 22, your brother will rise again. And Martha gives a very good answer, a good theological sound answer, a good answer from someone who was raised in Jewish Sabbath school. She says, yes, I know the prophets talk about a great resurrection on the last day. I know that Lazarus will be raised on the last day. But I wonder if you kind of hear what she leaves unsaid. Yes, I know he'll be raised. You didn't answer my question though, Jesus. Why didn't you come right away? Why did you permit this to happen?

And notice what Jesus says. He says, no, no, no, Martha. Your faith can't only be in a far off future event. Your faith needs to be in me. And he says:

> "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die." (John 11:25-26)

He makes it all about him. He's showing Martha that the promise of the resurrection life that was prophesied by the prophets of old, it culminates in a person. And that person is him, friends. Now that that person has arrived, our faith must be him. He's saying, your faith can't be just an event. Your faith needs to be in a person. You need to know that person. You need to love that person. You need to trust that person. And he puts it in such personal terms.

And then he puts the question to Martha: "Do you believe this?" He's saying, do you believe me? This is actually the answer to her question. Where were you? Why did you take so long? Why did you do this? And he simply says, do you trust me? Do you trust me? I'm what you need, Martha. I'm what your sister needs. I'm what everyone needs. And the people would not have seen it. They would not have believed it unless they witnessed me call forth a man from the grave who had been dead for four days. Do you trust me on this, Martha?

Could it not be, dear friend, that right now Jesus is putting you in a holding pattern, that he's waiting as it were because he has something bigger and better to accomplish in your life than the meager thing you've been praying for? Of course, praying that their brother would be healed would hardly seem to be a meager thing. They had no idea what Jesus was about to do. Could it be that Jesus is calling you to wait because he has something glorious planned for you? And he's asking you today, do you trust me? Do you trust me?

He only permits suffering and sadness in his people after he has already determined to perform their deliverance from that suffering and from that sadness. And it's a deliverance that will glorify God and will strengthen our faith. And his question to us is, do you trust me? Do you believe me?

Why does Jesus wait? Jesus waits so that God would be glorified and our faith would be strengthened in the demonstration of his power. Do you believe that?

I wanna give you a reason to believe it this morning because you might be hearing it and you might be saying, well, this all sounds well and good, pastor, but in my life, I feel like he's got a bad track record. So many prayers unanswered, so many disappointments in my life. And what you're saying sounds good, but how can I really know? How can I really believe he'll show up when I need him most? Because sometimes I feel like he hasn't. How can I know that those disappointments are actually preparing me for some great deliverance? How can I trust him? How can I know?

## Why Does Jesus Weep?

I wanna give you a reason to trust him and it's from our text. It's the second question I want us to ask of this text. First we said, why did Jesus wait? And now I want us to ask, why does Jesus weep?

Right there in verse 35, you're gonna find everything you need to put your trust in the plans of Jesus. What happens here? Jesus is told that Lazarus has been laid in a tomb and his response is to cry.

> "Jesus wept." (John 11:35)

Why should we believe that Jesus can and will perform a freeing deliverance in our lives? Because friends, every fiber of his heart is united to you in your plight and he wants nothing more than to free you from it. And when he sees you suffering, he weeps. He weeps.

This passage is teaching us, friends, not only that he has power, right? Why does he wait? Because he's gonna show the power that he has been given of God to raise a dead man to life. He waits not just to reveal faith inducing, glorious power of God. We see in this passage, it's not just about his power. He's not just all power. He's also all pity. There's passion here, there's care, there's concern. He is all love. Did you see that in verse 36?

> "See how he loved him." (John 11:36)

He's full of love.

I want you to do something I wouldn't normally recommend people do, but pretend you're Jesus for a moment. Don't make a habit of doing that, but put yourself in Jesus's sandals at this moment. Would you have wept? If it was you, I don't think I would have. I think I would have seen the people and they're all distressed and I think I would have felt bad for them, but I would have said, well, you know, just give it a minute, he'll be home for dinner. I'm about to raise him back to life. And yet, even knowing that he's about to bring this man out of the grave, Jesus still weeps over the grave.

Friends, your savior is not a cold, sterile solution to your sin and suffering. No, he is the friend of sinners. He is the man of sorrows. He is our great high priest who has a fellow feeling with all our infirmities. And if he cares enough to weep over a man who is about to be raised from the dead, do you think he doesn't care about whatever you're going through right now? Whatever struggle you're facing? He has to care. He has to care. Why? Because in the profound mystery of the gospel, we've been united to him and he has been united to us. He's our head, we're his body.

And as some of you have learned by doing some house projects over the years, when you're holding the nail and you're swinging the hammer, when the hammer hits the thumb, the brain doesn't say, well, at least it was just the thumb, not the brain. No, but the brain tells you that something very precious to you is in a lot of pain. And you should say, ouch!

In our head, in heaven, feels the pain of his members and is moved to pity. He's not just moved to pity. He's moved to do something about it.

See, the way I read this, it seems to me that the pity actually propels the power. It's the weeping at the grave that seems to catapult this cry from his voice:

> "Lazarus, come forth!" (John 11:43)

Right? How often have we been in situations where people come to us and they share a grief that they're going through, a conundrum they're faced with, a big question in life? They want advice, they need help. And how often have we sat there and we've listened and we've just thought, I have no idea what to say? I have no idea what to do. I feel so bad, but there's nothing I can do. Jesus doesn't have that problem. When he sees us in distress, he does something about it.

You don't want a savior who doesn't cry at the tomb, because that means he doesn't care for you. Nor do you want a savior who only can cry at the tomb, because that means he can't save you. But we have one who is all power and who is all pity, and these are joined together. We see that here at the tomb of Lazarus. He cries to him, calls to him. And just as the universe sprang into being at the summons of that same voice, Lazarus has to come out.

And this is the culmination of the love of Christ to you, dear Christian. If you are in Christ today, this is the culmination of his love to you. He will call you by name out of the grave on the last day. You will be raised. That's what Jesus said:

> "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live." (John 11:25)

How? Because one day I will call his name, one day I will call her name, they will come forth. His voice will awaken you from the sleep of death.

But friends, maybe his voice is calling you even right now. Maybe his voice is calling you right now, because before his voice can call you from the sleep of death, his voice needs to call you from the death of sin. Is there someone here today who needs to be converted? Is there someone who needs to be brought out of darkness, transferred from the domain of darkness into the kingdom of God's beloved Son in whom we have the redemption, in whom we have the forgiveness of our sins and our redemption? You can hardly imagine a better passage to draw you forth, brother or sister, than John 11.

### The Example of William Cowper

Our family has a deep affinity for William Cowper, the hymn writer. We appreciate him so much we named our second son, Caleb Cooper Cruz. We also call him cubed, because CCC. We love the story of Cowper. If you're not familiar with it, he struggled his whole life with depression, anxiety, and even lacking assurance of faith. But at one point in his 20s, he was placed in an insane asylum because of these bouts of depression and suicidal ideation he was having. And one day he's walking the grounds of the asylum and he comes across a Bible. The Bible is on a desk and it's open to John 11. It's not by accident. I don't just mean that in a Reformed way. What I mean is his doctor placed it there, open to John 11, hoping Cowper would come across it. And he did. And he read the story that we've read this morning.

And this is what William Cowper said about it:

> "I saw so much benevolence, mercy, goodness, and sympathy with miserable men in our Savior's conduct, that I almost shed tears upon the revelation of it, little thinking that it was an exact type of the mercy, which Jesus was about to extend towards me."

And he was converted later that day.

Do you see what Cowper saw? Do you see the benevolence? Do you see the mercy? Do you see the goodness? Do you see the sympathy of a Savior? Do you hear his voice calling you out of sin? Friend, if you hear his voice, you need to come to him and you come to him today, because when you come to him today, then you have the guarantee you will hear his voice on the last day, and you will come to him in resurrection life then as well.

## The Hope of Our Resurrection

One of my favorite things to do when I'm out late at a meeting is go home and check on the kids as they're sleeping, because I get to see something I never see when they're awake, which is just how angelic they are, and be reminded that this is worth it. But I have this sort of ritual or routine with my daughter. Dads and their daughters—that's different with my sons, but with Evie, I climb into bed next to her and I'll just kind of tap her gently. I'll just say, hey, Evie, Evie, just enough to get her to stir. And she opens her eyes, she smiles. And I say, daddy's home. And she gives me a kiss and goes back to sleep.

And I'll tell you, in that moment, she truly makes me to feel as if there's nothing better in all the world than to see her daddy.

Friends, that's what's awaiting you. If you are in Christ, death has become for us now a sleep. And one day we will hear the voice, the voice of our loving savior waking us up.

And David describes it like this in Psalm 17:

> "When I awake, I will be satisfied with your likeness." (Psalm 17:15)

We will see him, and all will be well.

What's your trouble today, dear friend? What are you waiting on the Lord for? You need to view this trouble in light of eternity. All right, the worst thing that can happen to you in life is that you die. And Jesus has defeated that problem. He is taking care of the worst thing that can happen to you. And if that's true, what about all the lesser things that you're going through? Will he not also take care of them for you?

If Jesus has solved the problem of death, he will solve the problem of your current suffering. And he has solved the problem. He's actually done more than just defeat death. He's completely transformed it. He's turned it into a sleep. And one day he will call you by name.

Lazarus, come forth.
Jonathan, come forth.
Nick, come forth.
Emily, come forth.

He'll call us by name, and we will awake.

Sometimes even the dulcet tones of daddy aren't enough to wake Evie up. And instead of the smile, I get a grumble, and she pulls the cover over her head. But who can say no to the authoritative voice of Almighty God? And who would ever want to resist the lovely voice of Jesus?

> "The sheep hear his voice. They know their shepherd, and they come to him." (John 10:27)

Oh friends, I preach to you today a savior who is full of pity, joined with power. The story of Lazarus gives us hope in our waiting on God. He's going to do something amazing, something greater than we could ever imagine. The story also gives us confidence in the love of a savior who is willing to weep because of our infirmities, and who would never cause you to shed a needless tear. The story also pictures for us what the end will be like for the Christian. But even then, only imperfectly. Even then, only imperfectly.

Our resurrection will be just like the resurrection of Jesus, not that of Lazarus. And there is one big difference. I wonder if you noticed it. Let me show it to you as we close. It's in verse 44:

> "The man who had died came out, his hands and feet were bound with linen strips or grave clothes, and his face wrapped with a cloth." (John 11:44)

Does this not give immense meaning to that otherwise obscure detail that we find in the Gospels about the first Easter Sunday? Do you remember it? It's in John's Gospel, in John chapter 20. Peter runs into the grave and he sees the grave clothes there. He sees the face cloth, not with the grave clothes, but folded up on its own. And you sort of wonder, why are we given that detail? But here we see the biggest difference between Lazarus' resurrection and between Jesus' and our resurrection.

Lazarus comes out with grave clothes because he will need them again. But Jesus—Jesus—now that he's been raised from the dead, will never die again. And neither will those who believe that he is the resurrection and the life.

Do you believe this?
